newsitem.title: USA: Japan's fiscal yearend seen as no bonanza for yen.
newsitem.headline: Japan's fiscal yearend seen as no bonanza for yen.

text.p: In a departure from the pattern that dominated the early 1990s, the yen has little hope of drawing strength from the upcoming end of Japan's fiscal year, according to market experts.

Though the dollar appreciation may entice some Japanese companies to sell U.S. assets in front of Japan's March 31 fiscal yearend, the meager return on Japanese investments will make the window-dressing swaps a mere book-keeping exercise with no lasting support for the yen, they predicted.

"I don't see the same yen strength related to yearend pressures. We're not looking at a scenario of yen repatriation," predicted Arthur Alexander, president of the Japan Economic Institute of America, a non-profit research group partly financed by Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
In the period from 1991 to 1996, a rising yen enjoyed a spring rally, spurring additional window-dressing selling of Japanese-held foreign assets.
"This year is quite different. More money is going abroad because of the very low returns in Japan," Alexander noted.

The meager yields on Japanese government securities -- 0.34 percent on the three-month bill to 2.47 percent on the 10-year issue -- and the faltering Nikkei stock index offer no incentive for Japanese firms to park funds at home.
"Foreigners are also leaving yen-based assets for these same reasons," Alexander added.
Low returns on Japanese assets also prevent Japanese companies from reaping the benefits tied to a weaker yen -- or liquidating overseas assets to beef up the foreign side of their balance sheets.

Nomura Securities International chief economist David Resler noted that, unlike with a strengthening yen, no rule requires Japanese firms to reflect on their balance sheets large foreign-exchange gains tied to a faltering yen.
"The foreign exchange rule that applies when the yen appreciates by at least 15 percent does not apply when the yen depreciates versus foreign currencies," Resler said.
Resler agreed that the sharp rise of the dollar versus the yen is unlikely to translate into liquidation of U.S. assets by Japanese holders due to the unappealing returns in Japan.

"If Japanese companies want to recognize their U.S. assets as valued at 120 yen instead of 105 to realize capital gains, they would have to sell them to do so," Resler said. "They can reinvest in U.S. assets right away and the net impact of the selling would not be significant with such swap transactions."
NatWest Markets vice president Satoshi Arisawa stressed return is a key consideration for Japanese pension managers who may only invest in yen or foreign fixed-income funds.
"Japanese pension funds managers are strongly requested to get higher return, meaning the allocation of money will continue to shift overseas," said Arisawa.

"They can sell the existing portfolio of foreign fixed-income markets, take the profits, and then reinvest. This does not affect the exchange rate," added Arisawa who cited the U.S. and U.K. fixed-income markets as the most attractive to Japanese funds managers.
Samuel Kahan, chief economist at the private firm A.S.K. Financial Research pointed out increasingly sophisticated derivatives would further lessen the impact of swaps.
"With swaps and derivatives, there are many ways of skinning the proverbial cat. There might be some quarter-end turbulence, but not a great amount," said Kahan.

"There still is a large group of people who think the dollar is overvalued and are fighting the trend. Once they realize the situation has changed, there will be a bigger move into dollars," Kahan further predicted.
"The world's portfolios are still underweighted in dollars. We can expect a sharp adjustment," Kahan added.
A senior executive at a Japanese insurance firm said the yen will likely continue to slide toward the fiscal yearend "because there is no constituency for a weaker dollar."

"Europe does not want a weaker dollar because of the European Monetary Union. Europe needs a strong dollar to counter the fiscal drag tied to the EMU criteria," said the executive who requested anonymity. "The United States wants a strong dollar to counter inflationary pressures."
The executive also said Japan would need to raise interest rates to prop up the yen -- an avenue that is closed due to the sluggish growth in Japan.
